text: Before you can protect Overlook's database, you need to actually stand it up. This lesson deploys the real Azure SQL Database this whole capstone is going to protect, using the same Azure CLI commands a production deployment would use.

Every Azure SQL Database sits inside a two-level hierarchy. The resource group holds everything together. The logical server — sql-overlook-capstone — owns the admin login, the firewall rules, and the public DNS name. And the database itself — db-overlook-core — owns its own compute and storage tier, and, importantly for this project, its own backup retention settings. Getting this split right matters, because later lessons touch settings at both levels.

Deploying both is two CLI commands. az sql server create sets up the logical server with an admin login. az sql db create creates the actual database inside it, on the General Purpose tier at 2 vCores — the standard production tier, sized appropriately for a real but modest workload, not over-provisioned and not under-provisioned.

Here's the detail worth sitting with before the next lesson. By deploying this as an Azure SQL Database — the PaaS tier — instead of SQL Server on a VM, you've already made a real decision about backups. Microsoft takes automated full, differential, and log backups on its own schedule. You don't get to run a raw BACKUP DATABASE statement against it the way you would on-prem. That's not a shortcut this capstone is taking — it's the accurate behavior of the platform you just chose, and it shapes exactly what the next several lessons look like.
The environment is live. Next lesson, you'll see exactly what a DBA still controls for backups on this platform — and what Azure has already taken off your plate.
